ticket.title: Foundation audit: two documented invariants are broken suite-wide, and no crate but workspace has a multi-repo test
acceptance_criteria:
CLAIMED AND BRANCHED 2026-11-07. Standing correction to how this ticket was worked: the earlier commits went straight to main with no claim and no InProgress transition, so the ledger could not say who was working or when.

BRANCH NOTE, so the claim does not overstate: `feat/gb-305-multi-repo-gate` is created in the meta-harness root, because the gate itself was a miter change that has already landed. The remaining work - four owed multi-repository tests - lands in four different repositories (benchwork-cli, storypole-cli, sawhorse-core, rabbet-cli), so each test gets its own branch in its own repository when it is written. A single branch name for four repositories would be a name that does not exist anywhere, which is precisely the kind of receipt this session has been removing.

REMAINING SCOPE, unchanged: the four owed tests. Everything else in this ticket is landed - the git boundary fix (3053b30), the layout gate's second half (2fabe8f), and the three reversion-proven multi-repository tests.

task.title: Foundation audit: two documented invariants are broken suite-wide, and no crate but workspace has a multi-repo test

acceptance_criteria:
AUDIT RUN 2026-11-06 across the seven foundation crates, plus the two invariants that cross repository boundaries. Two are broken, and one of them is the exact shape the workspace audit (GB-304) is looking for.

FOUNDATION HEALTH, measured (LOC, IO primitives, suite deps, stringified-error sites):
  crate                      LOC  fs proc env  gb-deps
  gaugeblock-contracts      1547   0    0   0        0
  gaugeblock-git             816   0    2   0        0
  gaugeblock-inventory      1039   6    1   1        1
  gaugeblock-mcp             473   0    0   0        0
  gaugeblock-security        610   0    0   0        0
  gaugeblock-syntax          272   0    0   0        1
  gaugeblock-workspace       632   5    0   3        2
That is healthier than expected. contracts does no IO and reads no clock or randomness, so its purity invariant holds. mcp holds no IO because it takes reader and writer, which is the right shape. security touching no environment variable is worth a second look later - a secret store that never reads env may be one that never gets a secret - but nothing there violates a written rule.

BROKEN INVARIANT 1 - one process boundary for git. SPEC.md says gaugeblock-git is the only crate that spawns git. It is not:
  outfeed/crates/outfeed-core/src/git/mod.rs:106      Command::new("git")
  outfeed/crates/outfeed-core/src/git/history.rs:41   Command::new("git")
The detail that makes this the interesting case: outfeed-core ALREADY depends on gaugeblock-git (its manifest line 14). So this is not a missing dependency that someone would notice - the crate has the foundation, and re-implemented a git call beside it anyway. That is precisely the 'depends on it' versus 'uses it fully' gap this audit exists to find, one crate lower down the stack than expected.
The remaining hits in the tree are test fixtures (miter's live under src/sandbox/tests/, which is test code despite the path), so the production code has exactly one legitimate spawner and two illegitimate ones.

BROKEN INVARIANT 2 - no tests can tell a repository from a suite. Multi-repository fixtures exist in exactly one crate:
  common/crates/gaugeblock-workspace   topology_fixture.rs, paths_fixture.rs
Nothing else in twelve repositories has a test where two repositories are in scope at once. This is the structural reason the three defects of the last two days reached production: benchwork tailing one telemetry log (GB-293), miter's dirty check blind to member repositories (GB-301), the index baseline written by no path that ran (GB-302). In each case every test had exactly one repository, and with one repository per-repository logic and suite logic are indistinguishable - so the tests passed and the code was wrong.

THE MIRRORING THESIS, which is why this audit is worth doing rather than chasing instances: these defects are not copy-paste. They are independently written from the same wrong premise ('the workspace is the repository I was launched in'), under time pressure, by work that optimises for the smallest diff that satisfies the ticket. Auditing one repository finds one instance; auditing the invariant finds the class. The four properties in GB-304 are the same method applied to paths; this ticket applies it to the git boundary and to test scope.

DURABLE MECHANISMS, in the order they pay off:
1. A test-scope rule: any crate that consumes WorkspaceTopology or GaugeblockPaths must have at least one test with two repositories in scope. Enforceable as a docs-check-style audit, and it is the single highest-value item here because it prevents the class rather than the instances.
2. A git-boundary gate: in production code (src/, excluding test directories) only gaugeblock-git may construct a git command. Same shape as the layers allowlist, with an allowlist for the foundation crate itself.
3. Fold 1 and 2 into whatever mechanism GB-304's gate ends up being, rather than shipping three audits.

NOT FIXED IN THIS PASS, deliberately. Moving outfeed's two git calls onto gaugeblock-git is small, but it is a separate atomic change in a crate this session has already restructured twice, and doing it here would bundle an unrelated edit into an audit commit.

ITEM 1 CLOSED 2026-11-06, commit 3053b30 (outfeed). The git process boundary holds again: the only spawn site in production code is gaugeblock-git/src/repo.rs.

outfeed-core's two direct spawns now go through gaugeblock_git::run_git - the log range read in git/history.rs and the staging call in git/mod.rs. The interesting part is unchanged from the audit: this crate already depended on gaugeblock-git and re-implemented the call beside the dependency, so the defect was invisible to a dependency check. That is the same shape GB-304 is looking for one crate lower in the stack, and the reason both audits exist.

One behaviour tightened rather than preserved, deliberately: the log output was decoded lossily and is now required to be UTF-8, so a commit message that is not valid UTF-8 becomes a reported error instead of being silently mangled. The changelog is generated from that text, so a quiet substitution would surface as wrong prose rather than as a failure. The `git add -A` hazard note from GB-150 is preserved verbatim, because moving the call must not quietly change what it stages.

Verification status, stated precisely: clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings clean, and outfeed-orchestrator 12/12 green including the test that had been failing. The full-workspace run was still compiling when I committed, because the build cache had been purged to clear a disk-space failure - see the environment note below. The suite run should be re-confirmed on the next pass rather than assumed.

ENVIRONMENT FINDING, which cost more time than the fix: the machine reached 99 percent disk with a 23 GB shared target directory at the suite root, and outfeed's release pipeline has a disk-space guard that refuses to run below about 3.7 GB free. So a correctness change appeared to fail because of the machine. Two lessons, both mine: purging the target directory in the background while a cargo build was writing into it produced a pile of 'no such file or directory' compile errors that looked like a code fault; and a build cache at the suite root has no Cargo.toml to clean, so it has to be removed by path.

ITEM 2 REMAINS - the multi-repository test gap. Nothing but gaugeblock-workspace has a test with two repositories in scope, and that is the mechanism that would have caught the three defects of this session. It is the higher-value half of this ticket and it is still open.

ITEM 2 STARTED 2026-11-07, commit 423c294 (outfeed). First multi-repository test in the suite outside gaugeblock-workspace.

WHAT IT DOES: creates a main checkout with a storypole ledger and a linked worktree that deliberately has no `.gaugeblock` of its own, then asserts that resolving from the worktree lands on the main checkout rather than on nothing. That second clause is the defect: the old upward walk found nothing there, so a release started in a worktree recorded no ticket and nothing reported it.

PROVEN LOAD-BEARING, which is the part that matters. With the pre-fix implementation restored the test fails - 'a worktree must find the main checkout's ledger, not nothing' - and with the current implementation it passes. A regression test never seen to fail is a test never shown to test anything, and this session has produced enough tests that passed against wrong code.

The fixture asserts git's exit status too, because a silently broken fixture makes a failing assertion look like a product defect. Same confusion one level up from the thing being tested.

THE RULE THIS INSTANTIATES, to be enforced next: any crate that consumes GaugeblockPaths or WorkspaceTopology needs at least one test where two repositories are in scope. With one repository, per-repository logic and suite logic are indistinguishable, which is how benchwork tailed one telemetry log, miter's dirty check missed member repositories, and this ledger walk silently returned nothing.

HOW TO ENFORCE IT, sketched from what the layout gate taught us: scan each crate's manifest for gaugeblock-workspace or gaugeblock-inventory, scan its tests for a two-repository fixture (git worktree, a second repository, or WorkspaceTopology), and fail when the first is present and the second is not - with an allowlist for crates whose dependency is a type import rather than a path question. That last distinction is the hard part: gaugeblock-contracts depends on nothing and uses neither, while chalkline-core may consume a type without ever resolving a path, and demanding a multi-repo test of it would be noise that teaches people to ignore the gate.

Honest ordering: build the check after a second and third crate have real multi-repo tests, so the pattern is proven by use rather than guessed. The candidates, in order of what broke: benchwork-core (telemetry tail), miter-engine (dirty detection), storypole-core (ledger).

ITEM 2, SECOND INSTANCE 2026-11-07, commit 4aaa772 (miter-engine). Two multi-repository tests now exist outside gaugeblock-workspace, both proven load-bearing by reversion.

  outfeed-orchestrator (423c294)  a linked worktree resolves to the main checkout's ledger; fails with 'must find the main checkout's ledger, not nothing' when the old upward walk is restored.
  miter-engine        (4aaa772)  a saved index remembers every file it describes; fails with 'both files are recorded - left: 0' when the baseline write is disabled.

Both tests use two repositories because the defects required two: with one repository in scope an empty baseline and a complete one are indistinguishable, a worktree and its main checkout are the same directory, and per-repository logic is correct by definition.

WHY REVERSION MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: this session has produced several tests that passed against wrong code - the archive sweep looked like it had failed because a filter widened silently, and three defects reached production behind green suites. A regression test that has never been observed to fail has not been shown to test anything, so both of these were run against the pre-fix implementation and observed to fail before being committed.

THE RULE IS NOW MODELLED ON PRACTICE rather than guessed: a crate consuming path or topology resolution needs a test with two repositories, and the two instances show what such a test looks like - a second repository, or a worktree of the first, plus an assertion that would fail if the resolution collapsed to one.

NEXT, in the order the defects happened: benchwork-core (the telemetry tail that read one repository of twelve), then storypole-core (the ledger). The benchwork one cannot pass today - the aggregation does not exist - so it stays a specification until GB-293 is fixed rather than a test that quietly asserts the bug.

STILL DEFERRED, deliberately: the gate that enforces this rule. Two instances is enough to model it on practice but not enough to know which crates the rule should exempt - chalkline-core may consume a type without resolving a path, and a gate that demands multi-repo tests of those would be noise, and noise is what teaches people to ignore gates.

ITEM 2, THIRD INSTANCE 2026-11-07, commit 588829d (storypole-core). Three multi-repository tests now exist, all proven load-bearing by reversion - and this one found a live defect rather than pinning a fix.

THE DEFECT: StorypoleStore::open walks upward to the nearest enclosing store. Correct for a command run from src/deep/ - the store belongs to the repository above. Wrong for a repository nested inside another: the walk leaves the child, finds the parent's store, and the child's work is recorded in the parent's ledger. Nothing reports it and the ledger looks exactly as it should.

The fix compares two answers rather than trusting one: the directory the walk found, and the repository git says the caller is in. When they differ, open refuses with Uninitialized - a visible failure instead of silent misattribution. The comparison is skipped when the caller is not in a git repository, so a plain directory tree behaves as before.

A NOTE ON THE FIRST VERSION OF THE TEST, because it nearly cost the finding: it created the child as a directory inside the parent and asserted the child must not adopt the parent's ledger. That was wrong - a directory inside a repository is not a repository, so inheriting is correct there - and the test failed for the right reason against a correct implementation. The fixture now runs git init in the child. A test whose premise is wrong looks exactly like a defect until you check which one is lying.

THREE INSTANCES, THREE DIFFERENT SHAPES OF THE SAME RULE:
  outfeed-orchestrator  a worktree resolves to its main checkout (second repository, different layout)
  miter-engine          a saved index remembers both members' files (two repositories, one database)
  storypole-core        a nested repository refuses its parent's ledger (two repositories, one inside the other)
That spread is what makes the rule defensible: 'a test with two repositories in scope' is not a slogan, it is three concrete fixtures showing what the assertion looks like when the code collapses to one.

STILL DEFERRED, and now with better evidence: the gate that enforces the rule. Three instances is enough to model it, but the exemption question is unresolved - chalkline-core may consume a type from gaugeblock-contracts without ever resolving a path, and demanding a multi-repo test of that is noise. The next useful step is not the gate but the fourth instance where the defect actually happened: benchwork-core's telemetry tail, which cannot pass until GB-293 exists, and therefore stays a specification rather than a test that asserts the bug.

GATE ENABLED 2026-11-07. `miter audit --paths` now enforces both halves of the adoption rule, and the tree passes both:

  AUDIT PASSED: No files exceed 250 lines
  AUDIT PASSED: every crate naming .gaugeblock depends on gaugeblock-workspace      (GB-304)
  AUDIT PASSED: every crate resolving the suite has a multi-repository test        (GB-305)

It arrived through the existing --paths flag, so no chain entries and no configs changed - the gate that was already wired now checks twice.

GATE DESIGN, and the measurement that shaped it. Sixteen crates touch the resolver; eight call `GaugeblockPaths::discover` or `WorkspaceTopology::discover`. Scoping the rule to the callers rather than the touchers is what keeps it usable: `at(root).member("dado")` is arithmetic over a path the caller already has, while `discover` is the operation whose answer changes with the repository. A rule covering all sixteen would have flagged eleven crates on day one and taught people to ignore it.

A test declares itself with a `multi-repo:` marker. Three were marked: outfeed's worktree test, storypole-core's nested-repository test, benchwork's two-log test. Self-declaration was chosen over heuristics after testing them: 'contains worktree' and 'initialises git twice' both missed one of the three.

Four crates call discover with no such test, recorded as a DEBT REGISTER rather than a suppression, each with the ticket that owes one: benchwork-cli, storypole-cli, sawhorse-core, rabbet-cli. If that list grows, the rule is being negotiated with instead of enforced.

The checkers skip their own files, because a checker necessarily contains the patterns it looks for and scanning itself manufactured a finding that would otherwise have been hidden by allowlisting the crate - which would also hide real findings in that crate.

COST OF THE LAST HOUR, recorded because it is the same lesson twice: rustfmt broke the 250-line limit twice during this change - audit_paths.rs at 251 and audit_multi_repo.rs at 275 - because a file sitting at the boundary is pushed over by a reformat rather than by an edit. Both were fixed structurally by splitting detection from reporting, not by trimming comments. The line limit plus a formatter means 'just under' is not a stable state.

NEXT, and it is B per the sequencing agreed before this started: emission (GB-297 MCP seam, GB-298 gaugeblock-cli) so the telemetry work becomes a one-command change instead of a chain of prerequisites. The four owed multi-repository tests are the other half of this item and can be taken any time.

CLAIMED AND BRANCHED 2026-11-07. Standing correction to how this ticket was worked: the earlier commits went straight to main with no claim and no InProgress transition, so the ledger could not say who was working or when.

BRANCH NOTE, so the claim does not overstate: `feat/gb-305-multi-repo-gate` is created in the meta-harness root, because the gate itself was a miter change that has already landed. The remaining work - four owed multi-repository tests - lands in four different repositories (benchwork-cli, storypole-cli, sawhorse-core, rabbet-cli), so each test gets its own branch in its own repository when it is written. A single branch name for four repositories would be a name that does not exist anywhere, which is precisely the kind of receipt this session has been removing.

REMAINING SCOPE, unchanged: the four owed tests. Everything else in this ticket is landed - the git boundary fix (3053b30), the layout gate's second half (2fabe8f), and the three reversion-proven multi-repository tests.
